blocks.x: Introduction
Simple regression uses one regressor. Multiple regression uses several, $x_1,\dots,x_k$.
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\dots+\beta_kx_k+\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\Normal(0,\sigma^2).
The model is linear because it is linear in the parameters $\beta_j$. The regressors themselves may be squares, products or logarithms.
$\beta_j$ is the change in the mean response for a one-unit change in $x_j$, with the other regressors held fixed.
Models that look more complicated are still multiple linear regression models.
Cubic: $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\beta_3x^3+\varepsilon$. Set $x_1=x$, $x_2=x^2$, $x_3=x^3$.
Interaction: $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\beta_{12}x_1x_2+\varepsilon$. Set $x_3=x_1x_2$.

Second-order with interaction: $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\beta_{11}x_1^2+\beta_{22}x_2^2+\beta_{12}x_1x_2+\varepsilon$. This has five regressors. Its surface can be a mound, a saddle or a ridge, depending on the coefficients.
Any model linear in the $\beta$’s is a linear regression model, whatever the shape of the surface.
Interaction means the effect of $x_1$ depends on the level of $x_2$. In the model with $\beta_{12}$, $\partial\,\Exp(Y)/\partial x_1=\beta_1+\beta_{12}x_2$.
For $25$ wire bonds, regress pull strength $y$ on wire length $x_1$ and die height $x_2$. The normal equations are
The solution is $\hat\beta_0=2.26379$, $\hat\beta_1=2.74427$, $\hat\beta_2=0.01253$. The matrix formula $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\mathbf{y}$ gives the same values.

The error variance is $\hat\sigma^2=5.2364$. The standard errors are $\se(\hat\beta_0)=1.060$, $\se(\hat\beta_1)=0.09352$, $\se(\hat\beta_2)=0.002798$. The slopes are estimated precisely; the intercept less so.
Eight observations of a response $y$ with two coded regressors $x_1,x_2\in\{-1,+1\}$:
Least Squares Estimation of the Parameters
Given $n$ observations $(y_i,x_{i1},\dots,x_{ik})$, the least squares estimates minimise
L=\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(y_i-\beta_0-\sum_{j=1}^k\beta_jx_{ij}\Big)^2.
Setting each partial derivative to zero gives $p=k+1$ normal equations in $p$ unknowns. In matrix form they are short.
Matrix Approach to Multiple Linear Regression
Write

\mathbf{y}=\begin{pmatrix}y_1\\\vdots\\y_n\end{pmatrix},\quad X=\begin{pmatrix}1&x_{11}&\cdots&x_{1k}\\\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\1&x_{n1}&\cdots&x_{nk}\end{pmatrix},\quad\boldsymbol\beta=\begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\vdots\\\beta_k\end{pmatrix},\quad\boldsymbol\varepsilon=\begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon_1\\\vdots\\\varepsilon_n\end{pmatrix}.
The model is $\mathbf{y}=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon$. The $n\times p$ matrix $X$ is the design matrix.
If $X\T X$ is invertible (the columns of $X$ are linearly independent), then
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\mathbf{y}.
It is the unique solution of the normal equations $X\T X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=X\T\mathbf{y}$.
The fitted values are $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=H\mathbf{y}$, where $H=X(X\T X)^{-1}X\T$ is the hat matrix. The residuals are $\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}=(I-H)\mathbf{y}$.

$L=(\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta)\T(\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta)$ has gradient $-2X\T(\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta)$. This is zero at the stated $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$. The Hessian $2X\T X$ is positive definite, so this is the unique minimum.

$H$ is symmetric and idempotent ($H^2=H$), and $\tr H=p$. It is the orthogonal projection of $\R^n$ onto the column space of $X$. So $X\T\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{0}$: the residual vector is orthogonal to every column of $X$. With an intercept column, $\sum e_i=0$.
$SS_E=\mathbf{e}\T\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{y}\T\mathbf{y}-\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\T X\T\mathbf{y}$ and
\hat\sigma^2=MS_E=\frac{SS_E}{n-p},\qquad p=k+1\text{ parameters.}
The columns $\mathbf{1}$, $x_1$, $x_2$ are mutually orthogonal, so $X\T X=\diag(8,8,8)$ and $(X\T X)^{-1}=\tfrac18I$. Each coefficient is a simple average:
\hat\beta_0=\bar{y}=17.1,\qquad \hat\beta_1=\tfrac18\sum x_{i1}y_i=\tfrac{24.0}{8}=3.0,\qquad \hat\beta_2=\tfrac18\sum x_{i2}y_i=\tfrac{12.4}{8}=1.55.
The fitted equation is $\hat{y}=17.1+3.0x_1+1.55x_2$.
Properties of the Least Squares Estimators
Assume $\Exp[\boldsymbol\varepsilon]=\mathbf{0}$ and $\Cov[\boldsymbol\varepsilon]=\sigma^2I$. Then:

$\Exp[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\Cov[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}$. Let $C_{jj}$ be the $j$-th diagonal entry of $(X\T X)^{-1}$. Then $\Var[\hat\beta_j]=\sigma^2C_{jj}$ and $\se(\hat\beta_j)=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}$.
$\Exp[\hat\sigma^2]=\sigma^2$.
(Gauss–Markov) Among all linear unbiased estimators, $\hat\beta_j$ has the smallest variance.

If $\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\Normal(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2I)$, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\sim\Normal\big(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}\big)$, $(n-p)\hat\sigma^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-p}$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is independent of $\hat\sigma^2$.

(i) $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T(X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon)=\boldsymbol\beta+(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\boldsymbol\varepsilon$. So $\Exp[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\boldsymbol\beta$, and $\Cov[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\,\sigma^2I\,X(X\T X)^{-1}=\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}$.
(ii) $\mathbf{e}=(I-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ because $(I-H)X=0$. Then $\Exp(\mathbf{e}\T\mathbf{e})=\Exp[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\T(I-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon]=\sigma^2\tr(I-H)=\sigma^2(n-p)$.

(iv) $I-H$ projects onto a subspace of dimension $n-p$. In orthonormal coordinates adapted to that subspace, $\boldsymbol\varepsilon\T(I-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon/\sigma^2$ is a sum of $n-p$ squared independent standard normals. Also $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ and $\mathbf{e}=(I-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ are jointly normal and uncorrelated (since $X\T(I-H)=0$), so they are independent.
(iii) Any other linear unbiased estimator $A\mathbf{y}$ has $AX=I$. Write $A=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T+D$ with $DX=0$. Then $\Cov(A\mathbf{y})=\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}+\sigma^2DD\T\succeq\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}$.

In the running example, $C_{jj}=1/8$ for every coefficient, so $\se(\hat\beta_j)=\sqrt{0.5/8}=0.25$. The off-diagonal entries of $(X\T X)^{-1}$ are $0$, so $\hat\beta_1$ and $\hat\beta_2$ are uncorrelated. Every hat-matrix diagonal entry is $h_{ii}=\tfrac38$, and they sum to $p=3$.

sections.title: Hypothesis Tests in Multiple Linear Regression

blocks.x: Test for Significance of Regression
SS_T=\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2=\mathbf{y}\T\mathbf{y}-n\bar{y}^2,\qquad SS_R=\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\T X\T\mathbf{y}-n\bar{y}^2,\qquad SS_E=SS_T-SS_R.
Degrees of freedom: $n-1=k+(n-p)$.
To test $H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=\dots=\beta_k=0$ against $H_1:$ at least one $\beta_j\ne0$, use
F_0=\frac{SS_R/k}{SS_E/(n-p)}=\frac{MS_R}{MS_E}\sim F_{k,\,n-p}\ \text{ when }H_0\text{ is true.}
Reject $H_0$ if $f_0>f_{\alpha,\,k,\,n-p}$ (upper tail only).
R^2=\frac{SS_R}{SS_T},\qquad R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}=1-\frac{SS_E/(n-p)}{SS_T/(n-1)}.
$R^2$ never decreases when you add a regressor.
$R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$ penalises extra regressors and can decrease. Use it to compare models of different size.
$f_0=(91.22/2)/0.5=91.2$. Since $f_{0.05,2,5}=5.79$, reject $H_0$: at least one regressor is useful.
Tests on Individual Regression Coefficients and Subsets of Coefficients
To test $H_0:\beta_j=0$ against $H_1:\beta_j\ne0$, use $T_0=\hat\beta_j/\se(\hat\beta_j)\sim t_{n-p}$ when $H_0$ is true. Reject if $\abs{t_0}>t_{\alpha/2,\,n-p}$.
One-sided: reject $H_1:\beta_j>0$ if $t_0>t_{\alpha,\,n-p}$; reject $H_1:\beta_j<0$ if $t_0<-t_{\alpha,\,n-p}$.
This is a marginal test. It asks whether $x_j$ adds anything when all the other regressors are already in the model.
$t_0=3.0/0.25=12.0$ for $\beta_1$ and $1.55/0.25=6.2$ for $\beta_2$. Both exceed $t_{0.025,5}=2.571$, so both regressors are significant.
To test a subset of coefficients, use the extra sum of squares method.
Split $\boldsymbol\beta=(\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2)$, where $\boldsymbol\beta_2$ holds $r$ coefficients. Test $H_0:\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf{0}$.
Fit the full model and the reduced model (without $\boldsymbol\beta_2$).
The gain in the regression sum of squares is
SS_R(\boldsymbol\beta_2\mid\boldsymbol\beta_1)=SS_R(\text{full})-SS_R(\text{reduced})=SS_E(\text{reduced})-SS_E(\text{full}).
When $H_0:\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf{0}$ is true,
F_0=\frac{SS_R(\boldsymbol\beta_2\mid\boldsymbol\beta_1)/r}{MS_E(\text{full})}\sim F_{r,\,n-p}.
Reject $H_0$ if $f_0>f_{\alpha,\,r,\,n-p}$. When $r=1$, $F_0=T_0^2$, where $T_0$ is the $t$ statistic of that coefficient.

Does $x_2$ add anything to a model that already has $x_1$? The reduced model $\hat{y}=17.1+3.0x_1$ has $SS_R=72$. So $SS_R(\beta_2\mid\beta_1)=91.22-72=19.22$ and $F_0=19.22/0.5=38.4=6.2^2$. Since $f_{0.05,1,5}=6.61$, it is significant.
Here $n=25$ and $p=3$, so there are $22$ error degrees of freedom. $SS_T=6105.9447$, $SS_R=5990.7712$, $SS_E=115.1735$.
$f_0\approx572$, far above $f_{0.05,2,22}=3.44$. The regression is significant. This does not show the model is adequate for prediction; that needs the checks of Section 6.5.
$R^2=0.9811$ and $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}=0.979$. With wire length alone: $R^2=0.9640$ and $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}=0.962$. Adding die height raises $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$ too, so it is a real improvement.
For $H_0:\beta_2=0$: $t_0=4.4767>t_{0.025,22}=2.074$ ($P=0.0002$). Die height helps, given wire length. The partial $F$ is $t_0^2\approx20.0>f_{0.05,1,22}=4.30$: same conclusion.
More About the Extra Sum of Squares Method (CD Only)
With an orthogonal design (as in the running example), $SS_R(\beta_2\mid\beta_1)=SS_R(\beta_2)$. The contribution of each regressor does not depend on the order of entry.
With non-orthogonal data it does depend on the order, and the contributions do not add up to $SS_R$.
Sequential (“Type I”) sums of squares depend on the order of entry.
Partial (“Type III”) sums of squares measure each regressor given all the others. They match the $t$-tests.
The same framework tests any linear restriction $C\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{0}$:
F_0=\frac{(SS_E(\text{restricted})-SS_E(\text{full}))/r}{MS_E(\text{full})}.

sections.title: Confidence Intervals in Multiple Linear Regression

blocks.x: Confidence Intervals on Individual Regression Coefficients
A two-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval, with $\alpha/2$ in each tail, is
\hat\beta_j-t_{\alpha/2,\,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}\le\beta_j\le\hat\beta_j+t_{\alpha/2,\,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}.

One-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ bounds use $t_{\alpha,\,n-p}$ and one limit: upper $\beta_j\le\hat\beta_j+t_{\alpha,\,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}$, lower $\hat\beta_j-t_{\alpha,\,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}\le\beta_j$. The same change ($t_{\alpha/2}\to t_\alpha$, one limit) applies to the mean-response and prediction intervals below.
Confidence Interval on the Mean Response

At a point $\mathbf{x}_0=(1,x_{01},\dots,x_{0k})\T$ the mean response is $\mu_{Y|\mathbf{x}_0}=\mathbf{x}_0\T\boldsymbol\beta$. It is estimated by $\hat\mu=\mathbf{x}_0\T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$, with $\Var[\hat\mu]=\sigma^2\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0$.
\hat\mu_{Y|\mathbf{x}_0}\pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\,\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0}.
A prediction interval is always wider than the confidence interval on the mean response at the same point. It must also cover the variation of one new $Y$.
A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ prediction interval for a new observation at $\mathbf{x}_0$ is
\hat{y}_0\pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\big(1+\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0\big)}.

In several dimensions, a point can lie inside the range of each regressor on its own, yet far from the cloud of data as a whole. This is a hidden extrapolation. The quantity $h_{00}=\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0$ detects it: if $h_{00}>\max_ih_{ii}$, the point lies outside the regressor variable hull, and predictions there are unreliable.
Residual Analysis

The residuals $\mathbf{e}=(I-H)\mathbf{y}$ have $\Cov(\mathbf{e})=\sigma^2(I-H)$, so $\Var[e_i]=\sigma^2(1-h_{ii})$. Residuals at high-leverage points are artificially small. So we also use scaled residuals.
Standardised residual: $d_i=e_i/\hat\sigma$.
Studentised residual: $r_i=\dfrac{e_i}{\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2(1-h_{ii})}}$. It has about unit variance for every observation. A value with $\abs{r_i}>3$ is a potential outlier.

The plots of Chapter 5 still apply: normal probability plot, residuals against $\hat{y}_i$, residuals against each $x_j$ (curvature suggests a missing quadratic term), and residuals against time order.
The prediction residual $e_{(i)}=e_i/(1-h_{ii})$ is the error when observation $i$ is left out of the fit. The statistic $PRESS=\sum e_{(i)}^2$ measures how well the model predicts new data.
Influential Observations
The leverage of observation $i$ is $h_{ii}=\mathbf{x}_i\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_i$. It is the weight that $y_i$ has on its own fitted value, since $\hat{y}_i=\sum_jh_{ij}y_j$.
$0\le h_{ii}\le1$ and $\sum h_{ii}=p$, so the average leverage is $p/n$.
High leverage: $h_{ii}>2p/n$.
Cook’s distance
D_i=\frac{r_i^2}p\cdot\frac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}}
measures how much all the fitted values change when observation $i$ is deleted. $D_i>1$ marks an influential point.

An observation is influential when it has high leverage (unusual $x$) and a large residual. A high-leverage point exactly on the trend only sharpens the fit. An outlier at low leverage shifts the line little. Investigate influential points; do not delete them automatically.
Polynomial Regression Models
A curve can be fitted by adding powers of a regressor. The quadratic $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\varepsilon$ is linear in $(x,x^2)$, so everything above applies with $x_1=x$, $x_2=x^2$.
Guidelines:
Keep the degree low (2 or 3).
Keep the lower-order terms when you keep a higher-order term.
Centre $x$ (use $x-\bar{x}$). This reduces the strong correlation between $x$ and $x^2$, which makes $X\T X$ ill-conditioned.
Be very careful when extrapolating: polynomials behave wildly outside the data range.
An interaction term $x_1x_2$ lets the effect of $x_1$ depend on the level of $x_2$.
Categorical Regressors and Indicator Variables
A factor with $m$ levels needs $m-1$ indicator (dummy) variables.
For a two-level factor (machine A or B), let $x=0$ for A and $x=1$ for B. In $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x+\varepsilon$:
Machine A has intercept $\beta_0$. Machine B has intercept $\beta_0+\beta_2$. The lines are parallel.
$\beta_2$ is the difference between B and A at a fixed $x_1$.
Adding the product $x_1x$ allows different slopes.
For $m=3$ levels use two indicators. Using $m$ indicators together with an intercept makes $X\T X$ singular (the dummy-variable trap).
Selection of Variables and Model Building

With many candidate regressors we want a model that is simple yet predicts well. Adding regressors always lowers $SS_E$. But it also raises the variance of predictions and can fit noise (overfitting).

All possible regressions. Compare all $2^k$ models using $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$, $MS_E$, PRESS, Mallows’ $C_p=\dfrac{SS_E(p)}{\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{full}}}-n+2p$ (a good model has $C_p\approx p$), or AIC$=n\ln(SS_E/n)+2p$.

Stepwise methods. They use partial $F$-statistics with an entry threshold $f_{\mathrm{in}}$ and a removal threshold $f_{\mathrm{out}}$, where $f_{\mathrm{in}}\ge f_{\mathrm{out}}$. (Software often uses $\alpha=0.15$ to enter and remove, and $0.10$ for backward elimination.)

Stepwise regression: start with the regressor most correlated with $y$. At each step add the candidate with the largest partial $F$ if it exceeds $f_{\mathrm{in}}$, then delete any included regressor whose partial $F$ falls below $f_{\mathrm{out}}$. Stop when nothing can be added or removed.
Forward selection: only adds. It never checks earlier entries for removal. This is its weakness.
Backward elimination: start with all $K$ candidates and remove the one with the smallest partial $F$ if it is below $f_{\mathrm{out}}$. Repeat.
Because each chosen variable maximises $F$, the advertised significance level is not the true level. The degrees of freedom of $MS_E$ also change at each step.

Textbook recommendation. If the number of candidates is small, use all possible regressions with the minimum $MS_E$ and $C_p$ criteria. It finds the best equation by those criteria, which stepwise methods do not guarantee, and it is not distorted by dependence among regressors. For $C_p$, use $MS_E$ of the full model as the estimate of $\sigma^2$. A model with negligible bias has $C_p\approx p$. Choose the minimum $C_p$, or a slightly larger one with little bias.
Always check the final model with residuals, lack of fit and influence. Compare several methods: there may be no single “best” equation.

If you choose a model with the same data you then use to test it, the reported $t$, $F$ and $P$-values are too optimistic. The winner was chosen because it looked good. Validate on fresh data or by cross-validation (Chapter 14). Prefer subject knowledge to blind automation.
Multicollinearity
Multicollinearity means some regressors are nearly linear combinations of others, so $X\T X$ is nearly singular. The variance inflation factor of $x_j$ is
\mathrm{VIF}_j=\frac1{1-R_j^2},
where $R_j^2$ is the $R^2$ from regressing $x_j$ on the other regressors.
One can show $\Var[\hat\beta_j]=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{jj}}\mathrm{VIF}_j$, where $S_{jj}=\sum(x_{ij}-\bar{x}_j)^2$. So VIF is the factor by which collinearity inflates the variance.
Rule. $\mathrm{VIF}_j>10$ (that is, $R_j^2>0.9$) signals a problem. Some authors think $10$ is too liberal and use $4$ or $5$.

Symptoms. Large standard errors; coefficients that change sign with small changes in the data; a significant overall $F$ with no significant individual $t$’s; a very small eigenvalue of $X\T X$ (condition number $\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}>1000$).

Remedies. Add data that break the near-dependence (often impossible). Drop or combine redundant regressors (you lose their information). Centre the variables. Use ridge regression or principal components regression.

What still works. Predictions inside the range of the data can be fine, because $\mathbf{x}\T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ may be well estimated even when individual $\hat\beta_j$ are not. Extrapolation needs good individual estimates and usually fails.
Ridge Regression (CD Only)
For $\lambda\ge0$,
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_R=(X\T X+\lambda I)^{-1}X\T\mathbf{y},
with the regressors standardised and the intercept left unpenalised. It minimises $SS_E+\lambda\sum_{j\ge1}\beta_j^2$.
The ridge estimator is biased, but it has smaller variance. For a suitable $\lambda>0$ it has a smaller mean square error than least squares when collinearity is severe.
It shrinks coefficients towards zero, most strongly in directions where the data carry little information (the small singular values of $X$; see Linear Algebra, Chapter 17).

Choosing $\lambda$: solve for several values (on standardised data, usually $0<\lambda<1$) and plot the coefficients against $\lambda$. This plot is the ridge trace. Take $\lambda$ as small as possible while the estimates are stable, since variance falls and squared bias rises as $\lambda$ grows. Cross-validation is another way.
Nonlinear Regression Models (CD Only)

Some models are intrinsically nonlinear in the parameters, for example $Y=\theta_1\big(1-e^{-\theta_2x}\big)+\varepsilon$. The least squares estimates minimise $\sum\big(y_i-f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta)\big)^2$, but there is no closed-form solution. We iterate, for example by the Gauss–Newton method:
Linearise $f$ about the current estimate: $f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta)\approx f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta^{(m)})+J_i(\boldsymbol\theta-\boldsymbol\theta^{(m)})$.
Solve the resulting linear least squares problem for the step.
Repeat until the estimates stop changing.
Good starting values (from a transformation or from physical insight) matter. The usual $t$ and $F$ tests hold only approximately, for large $n$.

Model: $\mathbf{y}=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon$. Estimator: $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\mathbf{y}$. $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=H\mathbf{y}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\Col X$. $\hat\sigma^2=SS_E/(n-p)$ with $p=k+1$.
$\Cov[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}$ and $\se(\hat\beta_j)=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}$. Gauss–Markov holds. Normal errors give $t$ and $\chi^2$ distributions.

Overall test: $F_0=MS_R/MS_E\sim F_{k,n-p}$. Single coefficient: $t_0=\hat\beta_j/\se(\hat\beta_j)\sim t_{n-p}$. Subsets: partial $F$ with the extra sum of squares. Use $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$ to compare models.
Mean response: $\mathbf{x}_0\T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\pm t\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0}$. For a prediction, add $1$ under the root.
Diagnostics: studentised residuals, leverage $h_{ii}>2p/n$, Cook’s $D_i>1$, PRESS. Watch for hidden extrapolation.

Modelling: polynomial terms (centre them); indicator variables ($m-1$ for $m$ levels); selection by $C_p$, AIC or stepwise (the $P$-values are optimistic); multicollinearity ($\mathrm{VIF}>10$), with ridge as a remedy; Gauss–Newton for nonlinear models.

For the running example, construct the analysis of variance table, test $H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0$ at $\alpha=0.05$ and compute $R^2$ and $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$. Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\beta_2$.
For the running example, find the $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean response and the $95\%$ prediction interval at $(x_1,x_2)=(-1,1)$ and at $(0,0)$. Why is the second interval narrower?
Show that $H=X(X\T X)^{-1}X\T$ is symmetric and idempotent, that $\tr H=p$, and that $0\le h_{ii}\le1$. Show also that $(I-H)X=0$.

A regression with $n=25$ and $k=4$ regressors gives $SS_R=420$ and $SS_E=180$. Test the significance of regression, compute $R^2$ and $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$. Adding two more regressors raises $SS_R$ to $438$; test whether the two added regressors are jointly significant.
Regressing $x_3$ on $x_1,x_2$ gives $R_3^2=0.96$. Find $\mathrm{VIF}_3$ and explain what it implies for the standard error of $\hat\beta_3$ relative to uncorrelated regressors.

Write the design matrix for a model with one quantitative regressor $x$ and a three-level factor (levels A, B, C) with indicator variables, for the six observations $(x,\text{level})$: $(1,A),(2,A),(3,B),(4,B),(5,C),(6,C)$. Interpret each coefficient.
In a regression with $n=20$, $p=3$ one observation has $h_{ii}=0.62$ and studentised residual $r_i=2.1$. Compute Cook’s distance and decide whether it is influential; compare $h_{ii}$ with $2p/n$.

Show that for ridge regression with $X\T X=\diag(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_p)$ each coefficient is the least squares coefficient multiplied by $\lambda_j/(\lambda_j+\lambda)$, and describe what this does to coefficients whose regressors carry little information.
